items.sentence_raw: The fertile land of the Nile delta is being eroded along Egypt's Mediterranean coast at an astounding rate, in some parts estimated at 100 metres per year.

In the past, land scoured away from the coastline by the currents of the Mediterranean Sea used to be replaced by sediment brought down to the delta by the River Nile, but this is no longer happening.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'In the past, land scoured away from the coastline'* — **'scoured away'** means eroded, and this happened *'before the dams were built'*. **'Coastal erosion occurred'** matches this fact. The answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Up to now, people have blamed this loss of delta land on the two large dams at Aswan in the south of Egypt, which hold back virtually all of the sediment that used to flow down the river.
items.explain: Q14: You may get confused between headings about dams and their effect. The passage says the Aswan dams *'hold back virtually all of the sediment that used to flow down the river'* — this stopped the natural flow of sediment that worked for thousands of years. **'Interrupting a natural process'** matches this effect exactly. The answer is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: Before the dams were built, the Nile flowed freely, carrying huge quantities of sediment north from Africa's interior to be deposited on the Nile delta.
This continued for 7,000 years, eventually covering a region of over 22,000 square kilometres with layers of fertile silt .

Annual flooding brought in new, nutrient-rich soil to the delta region, replacing what had been washed away by the sea, and dispensing with the need for fertilizers in Egypt's richest food-growing area.

But when the Aswan dams were constructed in the 20th century to provide electricity and irrigation, and to protect the huge population centre of Cairo and its surrounding areas from annual flooding and drought, most of the sediment with its natural fertilizer accumulated up above the dam in the southern, upstream half of Lake Nasser, instead of passing down to the delta.

Q20: The passage says the dams were built to *'provide electricity and irrigation, and to protect Cairo from flooding and drought'* — there is no mention of increasing delta fertility as a reason. The question says the dams were built to make the delta more fertile, which is the opposite of the stated purposes. The answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Now, however, there turns out to be more to the story.
It appears that the sediment-free water emerging from the Aswan dams picks up silt and sand as it erodes the river bed and banks on the 800-kilometre trip to Cairo.

Daniel Jean Stanley of the Smithsonian Institute noticed that water samples taken in Cairo, just before the river enters the delta, indicated that the river sometimes carries more than 850 grams of sediment per cubic metre of water - almost half of what it carried before the dams were built.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says Stanley found Cairo water carries *'more than 850 grams of sediment per cubic metre — almost half of what it carried before the dams were built'*. Half of the original very high amount is still a relatively high level, so this matches the question statement. The answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: "I'm ashamed to say that the significance of this didn't strike me until after I had read 50 or 60 studies," says Stanley in Marine Geology.
"There is still a lot of sediment coming into the delta, but virtually no sediment comes out into the Mediterranean to replenish the coastline.
So this sediment must be trapped on the delta itself."
Once north of Cairo, most of the Nile water is diverted into more than 10,000 kilometres of irrigation canals and only a small proportion reaches the sea directly through the rivers in the delta.
items.explain: Q15: You may mix up headings about sediment and other delta problems. The passage says most Nile water goes into *'irrigation canals'*, and slow-moving canal water *'cannot carry sediment'*. **'Effects of irrigation on sedimentation'** describes this link perfectly. The answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: The water in the irrigation canals is still or very slow-moving and thus cannot carry sediment, Stanley explains.

items.sentence_raw: The sediment sinks to the bottom of the canals and then is added to fields by farmers or pumped with the water into the four large freshwater lagoons that are located near the outer edges of the delta.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says sediment is *'pumped with the water into the four large freshwater lagoons'* from the canals. This directly matches the question statement. The answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: So very little of it actually reaches the coastline to replace what is being washed away by the Mediterranean currents.

items.sentence_raw: The farms on the delta plains and fishing and aquaculture in the lagoons account for much of Egypt's food supply.
items.explain: Q16: You might mix up pollution effects with other issues. The passage says delta farms and fishing provide *'much of Egypt's food supply'*, and poisons in sediment *'affect the productivity of fishing and farming'*. **'The threat to food production'** matches this risk exactly. The answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: But by the time the sediment has come to rest in the fields and lagoons it is laden with municipal, industrial and agricultural waste from the Cairo region, which is home to more than 40 million people.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says sediment in the delta is *'laden with municipal, industrial and agricultural waste'* — these are **pollutants**. This matches the description of increased levels in delta silt. The answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: "Pollutants are building up faster and faster," says Stanley.
Based on his investigations of sediment from the delta lagoons, Frederic Siegel of George Washington University concurs.

"In Manzalah Lagoon, for example, the increase in mercury, lead, copper and zinc coincided with the building of the High Dam at Aswan, the availability of cheap electricity, and the development of major power-based industries," he says.
Since that time the concentration of mercury has increased significantly.
Lead from engines that use leaded fuels and from other industrial sources has also increased dramatically.
These poisons can easily enter the food chain, affecting the productivity of fishing and farming.

items.sentence_raw: Another problem is that agricultural wastes include fertilizers which stimulate increases in plant growth in the lagoons and upset the ecology of the area, with serious effects on the fishing industry.

According to Siegel, international environmental organisations are beginning to pay closer attention to the region, partly because of the problems of erosion and pollution of the Nile delta, but principally because they fear the impact this situation could have on the whole Mediterranean coastal ecosystem.
items.explain: Q17: You may confuse short-term and long-term focus here. The passage says organisations fear the *'impact this situation could have on the whole Mediterranean coastal ecosystem'*, and also mentions *'in the long term'* solutions like desalination. **'Looking at the long-term impact'** fits this focus. The answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: But there are no easy solutions.

In the immediate future, Stanley believes that one solution would be to make artificial floods to flush out the delta waterways, in the same way that natural floods did before the construction of the dams.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says *'in the immediate future, Stanley believes that one solution would be to make artificial floods'* — **'immediate future'** means short term. This directly matches the question's request for a short-term solution. The answer is **A**.
